title: Form Processing Patterns
subtopics: Preserving appropriate form values after errors
learning_outcomes: Explain the role of form processing patterns in a Classic ASP application.
Identify and describe at least two syllabus subtopics: Displaying an empty form and Processing a submitted form.
Inspect a minimal example and define a reproducible normal-case and failure-case test.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will study form processing patterns as part of Classic ASP development and legacy maintenance. The lesson follows the attached ASP curriculum topic 56 and uses the syllabus subtopics as the coverage checklist.
content.why_it_matters: Form Processing Patterns matters because Classic ASP behavior crosses a server-side scripting engine, IIS configuration, request/response boundaries, and often COM or ADO dependencies. A small, explicit test helps distinguish intended behavior from runtime-specific behavior.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Forms convert browser-controlled input into application actions. For 'Form Processing Patterns', validate on the server, validate against an allow-list where feasible, encode data when redisplaying it, and verify identity and authorization before a protected operation. A successful HTML form submission should have an explicit failure path and should not rely only on JavaScript or hidden controls.

content_blocks.title: Syllabus coverage
content_blocks.text: The lesson explicitly covers: Displaying an empty form; Processing a submitted form; Displaying validation errors; Preserving appropriate form values after errors; Successful submission handling; Post/Redirect/Get workflows; Preventing unintended duplicate submissions. Treat these subtopics as connected requirements. For each one, be able to define the concept, identify where it appears in a Classic ASP application, and name one test or diagnostic that would verify it.

content_blocks.title: Inspectable example: Form Processing Patterns
content_blocks.code:
<%
If UCase(Request.ServerVariables("REQUEST_METHOD")) = "POST" Then
  If Len(Trim(Request.Form("message"))) = 0 Then
    Response.Status = "400 Bad Request"
    Response.Write "Message is required."
    Response.End
  End If
  Response.Redirect "/feedback-thanks.asp"
End If
%>
content_blocks.expected_output: A successful POST redirects to a confirmation page; invalid input is rejected.
content_blocks.run_instructions: The redirect is an example of Post/Redirect/Get. State-changing requests still need correct authorization and CSRF protections. The standard CodeLeaf browser playground previews HTML/CSS/JavaScript only; it does not execute Classic ASP, VBScript, ADO, IIS commands, PowerShell, or SQL. This block is therefore marked for static inspection unless you run it in the clearly identified local tool.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the original sample and test data. Change one condition, input, provider setting, or runtime option at a time, then compare observed behavior with the expected result.
content_blocks.limitations: Not executed during course generation. Classic ASP examples require a configured Windows/IIS environment with the matching ASP scripting engine and any required COM/ADO providers. Provider-specific and IIS-version-specific behavior must be verified locally.

content_blocks.title: Runtime and safety checkpoint
content_blocks.text: Submit requests through a browser to a local/test IIS site. Test missing fields, repeated parameters, session expiry, and a second request; do not infer security from a successful happy path. The source syllabus treats Classic ASP as a legacy maintenance technology, not as ASP.NET or a default choice for new web projects.

content_blocks.title: Guided workflow
content_blocks.text: 1. Start with a minimal local example of form processing patterns. 2. Trace its inputs, state changes, dependencies, and output. 3. Test a normal case, a missing/malformed case, and one permission/provider/runtime failure. 4. Write down the exact expected and observed result before changing another variable.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Create a small, reviewable demonstration of form processing patterns using synthetic data. Include at least one of these syllabus concepts: Displaying an empty form. State the expected result first, then add one invalid or boundary case and explain how your program should behave.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating legacy runtime behavior as universal.
common_mistakes.why: IIS versions, Windows lifecycle, COM registration/bitness, and ADO providers can change behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Write down the actual server/provider versions and validate on a disposable test site.

common_mistakes.why: Empty input, missing records, expired sessions, permissions, timeouts, and malformed data reveal different failure modes.
common_mistakes.fix: Add normal, negative, and boundary cases with expected outcomes.

common_mistakes.why: Detailed errors can reveal paths, SQL text, configuration, and component information.
common_mistakes.fix: Keep diagnostics in restricted server-side logs and return a generic message with a reference ID.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming syntax alone proves the application works.
common_mistakes.why: IIS configuration, permissions, COM activation, database providers, and response behavior are external dependencies.
common_mistakes.fix: Run against the documented local test host and record exact evidence.

common_mistakes.why: Query strings, form fields, cookies, and hidden controls remain client-controlled.
common_mistakes.fix: Validate on the server and apply authorization and output encoding at the appropriate boundary.
